book.title: Operation SINDOOR: The Untold Story of India's Deep Strikes Inside Pakistan
book.author: Lt Gen K.J.S. Dhillon (Retd)
book.note: A first-hand Indian account by a retired Indian Army officer who commanded XV Corps in Kashmir and served as Director General of Military Intelligence. Detailed, named and checkable — and an Indian account, not a neutral history.

method: Facts read out of the book and typed here by hand, then verified: each carries a phrase that must still appear in the book, and the run fails if any does not. Page numbers are not typed at all — each is read from the nearest print-page anchor in the EPUB, so a citation cannot drift from what it cites. Coordinates are fetched from Wikipedia, never entered here.
refusal: This is one side's account, by a retired Indian Army officer, and is published as such. No casualty figure and no aircraft-loss total appears here for either country, because those are exactly where the two national accounts diverge and neither can be checked.

tiers.india-official: Quoted from an Indian government briefing or from Parliament. India saying what India did.
tiers.author: The author's own first-hand account.
tiers.pakistan-concession: A Pakistani source stating something against Pakistan's own interest — the strongest evidence available in this conflict, because it costs the speaker something.
tiers.third-party: A foreign analyst with no stake in either account.
tiers.contested: The two national accounts conflict. Recorded as a conflict, not resolved.

cannotSay: What happened. This is what one well-placed Indian participant says happened, checked against his own text rather than against the events. A book verifying against itself is a guarantee about the citation, not about the claim.
What either side lost. No casualty figure and no aircraft-loss total is published here. Both governments have the strongest possible reason to shade those, and no independent count exists.
That a site named here was what the book says it was. The descriptions of who used each camp are the author's attributions, published as his and not as findings.
Anything about Pakistan's account, which is not in this book and is not in this file. The /sindoor page holds statements from both and keeps them apart.

beats.label: Pahalgam
beats.what: The attack on civilians at Pahalgam, which the book treats as the trigger for everything that follows.

beats.label: Nine sites, one night
beats.what: Nine sites struck. Seven engaged by the Indian Army with long- and medium-range weapons along the Line of Control and international border; two — Muridke and Bahawalpur — engaged by the Indian Air Force in depth.
beats.verify: seven were engaged by the Indian Army and two were engaged by the IAF
beats.chapter: 4. The War Room: Preparation and Strike

beats.label: The aircraft that struck nothing
beats.what: Aircraft simulated activity along the whole front to divide and stretch Pakistani reaction forces, so the defences could not concentrate on the actual strike.
beats.verify: simulated activity continuously along the entire front
beats.chapter: 4. The War Room: Preparation and Strike

beats.label: Three waves, forty launch points
beats.what: More than 300 drones launched from Pakistani territory within six hours, in three waves from nearly forty locations, from the night of 8–9 May into the morning of 10 May.
beats.verify: in three waves from nearly forty locations

beats.label: Bunyan-al-Marsoos
beats.what: Pakistan named its campaign Bunyan-al-Marsoos, 'Unbreakable Wall', framed domestically as Marka-i-Haq, 'the Battle of Truth'.

beats.label: The airfields
beats.what: In the second half of the night of 9–10 May, India struck Pakistani airfields and radar sites, which the Ministry of External Affairs briefing of 10 May described as precision attacks on identified military targets only.
beats.verify: precision attacks only on identified military targets

beats.label: What India conceded
beats.what: The same Indian briefing stated that limited damage was sustained to equipment and personnel at Indian Air Force stations at Udhampur, Pathankot, Adampur and Bhuj.
beats.verify: limited damage was sustained to equipment and personnel

beats.label: A loss admitted
beats.what: Retired Pakistani Air Marshal Masood Akhtar told Pakistani media that an AWACS aircraft was damaged at Bholari when the fourth of four missiles hit its hangar.
beats.verify: the fourth one hit the hangar at Bholari airbase

beats.label: Eleven bases, in Parliament
beats.what: Indian Home Minister Amit Shah told Parliament on 29 July 2025 that eleven Pakistani airbases had been targeted, of which eight were hit.

beats.label: The ceasefire
beats.what: A ceasefire was announced in the late evening of 10 May 2025.
beats.verify: the ceasefire was announced on 10 May 2025 in the late evening

disputes.question: How many Pakistani drones were brought down?
disputes.indiaSays: The book puts it at approximately 900-plus between 7 and 10 May, naming Turkish-origin YIHA III, Asisguard Songar, Bayraktar TB2 and Akinci types.
disputes.note: An Indian estimate of its own air defence's performance. No independent count exists, and the figure is the kind that is hardest to check and easiest to round upward.

disputes.question: What did each air force lose?
disputes.indiaSays: The book records the Indian Chief of the Air Staff being quoted, and records a Pakistani Air Marshal admitting an AWACS was damaged at Bholari.
disputes.note: This is the single most disputed question of the four days and the one where both governments have the strongest reason to shade. The /sindoor page publishes no aircraft-loss total for either side, and neither does this.
disputes.verify: Ex-Pak Air Marshal Admits Losing AWACS Aircraft

disputes.question: Who brought about the ceasefire?
disputes.indiaSays: The book devotes a section to the question, titled 'The Ceasefire: Who Did It?'
disputes.note: Claimed by more than one party. Recorded here as a question the book asks, not as an answer this site adopts.

disputes.question: Did India strike Afghanistan?
disputes.indiaSays: The Indian Foreign Secretary called the Pakistani claim ludicrous and frivolous; the book records that the Taliban government also denied it.
disputes.note: A rare case in this conflict where a third party's denial lines up against the claimant rather than with it.
